## Official Topic

Handling many models.

## Problem Focus

How do we repeat one declared modeling workflow across groups without turning
different contexts into a misleading ranking?

Students extend the Week 13 `airquality` model across May through September.
They split one checked modeling table, fit the same formula to every month,
retain each model object, extract aligned summaries, preserve uncertainty and
diagnostic evidence, and repeat a sensitivity calculation.

::: {.callout-note}
Week 14 changes the group subset while holding the formula and result contract
fixed. It does not search a large space of formulas or choose a winner by one
training metric. Week 15 returns to communication and synthesis.
:::

## Learning Goals

By the end of the week, students should be able to:

- explain why a many-model workflow needs a fixed question and contract;
- create a checked grouping variable with an intentional order;
- split one modeling table into a named list of group tables;
- reconcile the number and names of groups before fitting;
- define a one-group modeling function with explicit input requirements;
- return the model object and one-row summary together;
- apply the function once per group with `lapply`;
- preserve one result record for every requested group;
- verify that every group used the same formula and variable meanings;
- extract aligned sample size, coefficient, interval, training metric, and
  diagnostic fields;
- compare point estimates while retaining uncertainty and group size;
- explain why models fitted to different subsets are not direct competitors;
- repeat standardized-residual and Cook's-distance checks by group;
- link every flagged diagnostic to the original observation identifier;
- perform one declared sensitivity refit per group;
- explain why lower error after deleting a difficult training row is not
  validation evidence;
- identify small-group instability in a repeated result table;
- audit an AI ranking that ignores sample size, uncertainty, diagnostics, and
  new-data evidence.

## Supplied Material

Week 14 uses the built-in `airquality` data and the Week 13 formula

```r
ozone_ppb ~ temperature_f + wind_mph
```

Recommended structure:

```text
week14/
  week14-many-models.R
  week14-grouped-sensitivity.R
```

## Meeting 1: One Contract, Several Groups

**Question:** Which parts of the workflow must remain identical before monthly
model summaries can be placed in the same table?

Suggested 75-minute rhythm:

| Time | Activity |
|---:|---|
| 0-10 min | Restate the Week 13 model and comparison limits |
| 10-22 min | Build an ordered month factor and checked modeling table |
| 22-35 min | Split data and reconcile group names and row counts |
| 35-50 min | Write and test `fit_one_month` on May |
| 50-62 min | Apply the function to all five months and retain model objects |
| 62-70 min | Combine aligned summaries and plot coefficients with intervals |
| 70-75 min | Exit ticket: what must stay fixed across all five fits? |

### Start From One Checked Table

```r
model_data <- airquality |>
  transmute(
    observation_id = row_number(),
    month = factor(month.abb[Month], levels = month.abb[5:9]),
    ozone_ppb = Ozone,
    temperature_f = Temp,
    wind_mph = Wind
  ) |>
  filter(complete.cases(ozone_ppb, temperature_f, wind_mph))
```

The observation unit and complete-case rule are identical to Week 13.

### Split Into A Named List

```r
month_data <- split(model_data, model_data$month)
```

The list has five elements named `May`, `Jun`, `Jul`, `Aug`, and `Sep`. Each
element is a data frame containing one month's observations.

Check before modeling:

```r
stopifnot(
  identical(names(month_data), month.abb[5:9]),
  sum(vapply(month_data, nrow, integer(1))) == nrow(model_data)
)
```

### Freeze The Formula

```r
fixed_formula <-
  ozone_ppb ~ temperature_f + wind_mph
```

Changing both subset and formula would make the source of differences harder
to identify. Week 14 holds the formula fixed.

### One-Group Function Contract

`fit_one_month` requires:

- a data frame with the declared columns;
- exactly one month;
- at least five complete observations;
- variation in both predictors;
- the fixed formula.

It returns a list containing the month name, formula, fitted `lm` object, and
one-row summary.

### Test One Group Before Repeating

```r
may_result <- fit_one_month(
  month_data[["May"]],
  "May",
  fixed_formula
)
```

Inspect the fit class, row count, coefficient names, interval bounds, and
training metric before running all groups.

### Repeat The Checked Unit

```r
model_results <- lapply(
  names(month_data),
  function(month_name) {
    fit_one_month(
      month_data[[month_name]],
      month_name,
      fixed_formula
    )
  }
)
names(model_results) <- names(month_data)
```

The outer list preserves one complete modeling result for each requested month.

### Extract Comparable Summaries

```r
model_summary <- bind_rows(lapply(
  model_results,
  function(result) result$summary
))
```

Each row retains:

- month and sample size;
- temperature coefficient and 95% interval;
- wind coefficient;
- training RMSE;
- training R-squared.

### Check Group Accounting

```r
stopifnot(
  nrow(model_summary) == length(month_data),
  identical(model_summary$month, names(month_data)),
  sum(model_summary$n_observations) == nrow(model_data)
)
```

Five requested fits must produce five complete model records.

### Plot Estimates With Uncertainty

```r
ggplot(model_summary, aes(month, temperature_slope)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = temperature_low, ymax = temperature_high)
  ) +
  geom_point()
```

Point estimates without intervals invite overconfident comparisons.

### Different Subsets Are Not Competitors

The monthly fits describe different subsets and have sample sizes from 9 to 29.
A higher monthly R-squared does not mean that month “won” a common prediction
contest. The models did not predict the same observations.

## Meeting 2: Repeat Diagnostics And Sensitivity

**Question:** Does automation preserve the evidence that would make a monthly
coefficient fragile?

Suggested 75-minute rhythm:

| Time | Activity |
|---:|---|
| 0-10 min | Reconcile one model record per month |
| 10-25 min | Extract standardized-residual and Cook's-distance flags |
| 25-38 min | Link flags to original observation identifiers |
| 38-52 min | Remove one declared high-residual row and refit each month |
| 52-62 min | Compare original and sensitivity slopes and training RMSE |
| 62-70 min | Audit an AI ranking based only on training R-squared |
| 70-75 min | Exit ticket: evidence that prevents a false winner |

### One Diagnostic Record Per Group

For every month, retain:

- number of observations;
- count of standardized residuals beyond -2 or 2;
- count above the classroom Cook's-distance threshold;
- original identifier of the selected sensitivity row;
- original and sensitivity coefficients;
- original and sensitivity training RMSE.

Do not keep only the months that look well behaved.

### Preserve Source Identifiers

```r
removed_index <- which.max(abs(rstandard(fit)))
removed_id <- data$observation_id[[removed_index]]
```

List positions change after filtering or splitting. The original identifier is
the durable link back to the source observation.

### Declared Sensitivity Refit

```r
sensitivity_data <- data[-removed_index, , drop = FALSE]
sensitivity_fit <- lm(fixed_formula, data = sensitivity_data)
```

This is a deliberate “what changes?” calculation, not a rule that the removed
observation was wrong.

### Interpret Sensitivity, Not Just Fit

In three of the five monthly models, the temperature slope changes by more than
40% after removing the largest absolute standardized residual. June changes by
about 73% and has only nine complete observations.

That instability is evidence to report. It is not repaired merely because the
refitted training RMSE is lower.

### Why Training Error Falls

The sensitivity model omits a row selected because it was difficult for the
original fit. Lower training error on the smaller, changed dataset is expected
and is not a fair new-data comparison.

### Compare Patterns, Not Winners

Useful cross-group questions include:

- Are coefficient directions broadly consistent?
- Which intervals are wide?
- Which groups have small samples?
- Where do diagnostics or sensitivity reveal fragility?
- Which group differences merit contextual investigation?

“Which model is best?” is not well-defined when each model addresses a
different subset.

## AI-Aware Task: Ranking Can Destroy The Question

The generated review ranks months only by training R-squared and declares
September the best. It then treats June's positive wind coefficient as causal
and claims the ranking will hold on future observations.

The audit checks that:

1. monthly models use different observations;
2. June has only nine rows;
3. June's wind interval includes zero;
4. every month has at least one diagnostic flag;
5. three temperature slopes change by more than 40% in sensitivity fits;
6. no new-data evidence appears in the ranking.

## Project 2 Connection

Week 14 reinforces Project 2 habits:

- keep the declared formula stable after the plan is frozen;
- preserve one result record for each requested task;
- link diagnostics and predictions to source identifiers;
- run the declared sensitivity procedure;
- distinguish training changes from validation evidence;
- report instability instead of hiding it.

The monthly many-model analysis is a teaching example, not an additional
Project 2 requirement.

## Survival Checklist

### Commands And Patterns To Own

| Pattern | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `split(data, data$group)` | create one named data frame per group |
| `lapply(groups, fit_function)` | run one checked fit per group |
| `list(fit = fit, summary = row)` | retain model and aligned evidence |
| `confint(fit)` | calculate coefficient intervals |
| `bind_rows(summary_list)` | combine compatible one-row summaries |
| `vapply(results, ..., character(1))` | verify a scalar contract across fits |
| `which.max(abs(rstandard(fit)))` | locate a declared sensitivity row |

### Before Repeating Models

- Fix the question, formula, variables, units, and cleaning rule.
- Check group names, order, row counts, and predictor variation.
- Test the one-group function on a known group.
- Declare the complete result schema.
- Decide how a failed group will remain visible.

### Before Comparing Results

- Reconcile requested groups and returned records.
- Retain sample size and uncertainty beside coefficients.
- Label all training metrics explicitly.
- Preserve diagnostic counts and source identifiers.
- Inspect sensitivity changes, not just refitted error.
- Ask whether models use the same observations before ranking them.
- State what new-data evidence is absent.
